summary: This informational document introduces existing mechanisms that can be used for IPv6 site renumbering and covers many of the issues and requirements. It is a gap analysis organized by the main steps of renumbering, providing a basis for future work on solutions.

plainLanguage.summary: Changing every device's address in a network is hard. This lists the steps and where the tools are missing.

what are the challenges in ipv6 renumbering
what renumbering gaps still need solutions

subtitle: Challenges and tools for changing the IP addresses of all devices in an IPv6 network.

tldr.problem: Renumbering an IPv6 site (changing all devices' addresses) is painful and expensive, discouraging network managers from renumbering. Yet widespread use of Provider-Independent (PI) addressing to avoid renumbering creates BGP scaling problems.
tldr.mechanism: The document identifies gaps in existing mechanisms for automating the renumbering process, organized by renumbering steps: prefix management, address configuration, updating address-relevant entries, and renumbering event management.
tldr.outcome: While many tools and standards exist, significant gaps remain in automation, configuration management, DNS synchronization, and multicast handling. Some gaps are solvable with protocol changes; others are fundamental architectural limitations.

today: RFC 7010 is an Informational document providing a gap analysis of IPv6 site renumbering. It is not a standard or set of procedures, but rather an analysis intended to guide future work. The document builds on RFC 4192 (the make-before-break renumbering procedure) and RFC 5887 (an earlier statement that renumbering still needs work). It identifies issues that are solvable through protocol changes and those that are fundamental limitations.

sections.title: The Renumbering Problem
sections.content:
IPv6 site renumbering is the process of changing all the IP addresses in a network, typically when switching to a new Internet Service Provider (ISP). This is necessary but painful. Managers avoid renumbering by requesting Provider-Independent (PI) addressing, which does not need to change if they change providers. However, widespread PI addressing causes BGP routing table bloat.

Renumbering is expensive and error-prone because many devices and databases store IP addresses: routers, firewalls, servers, DNS records, application configurations, and monitoring systems. Coordinating changes across all these systems is complex. The make-before-break approach helps by running both old and new prefixes simultaneously during a transition period, allowing sessions to complete before old addresses expire.

This gap analysis examines existing tools and standards, identifies where automation is incomplete, and categorizes gaps as solvable or unsolvable.
sections.plainLanguage: When a company changes to a new Internet provider, all computers in the company need new addresses. That means updating the DNS, the firewall rules, server settings, and more. Many things can go wrong. IPv6 has some tools to help, but they don't do everything automatically.

sections.title: Existing Tools and Mechanisms
sections.content:
Several existing mechanisms can help with renumbering. Router Advertisement (RA) messages advertise new prefixes and deprecate old ones. Stateless Address Autoconfiguration (SLAAC) allows hosts to configure addresses automatically from RA prefixes. DHCPv6 can deliver addresses and can trigger reconfiguration. DHCPv6 Prefix Delegation (PD) allows routers to receive delegated prefixes automatically from upstream and distribute longer prefixes downstream.

IPAM (IP Address Management) tools integrate DHCP and DNS, making address coordination easier. Some vendors provide proprietary tools to push configuration changes. Configuration management tools like CFEngine can update multiple devices. The RFC 4192 procedure describes step-by-step how to renumber a site without a flag day.
sections.plainLanguage: IPv6 has Router Advertisements that can announce new addresses, automatic address configuration for computers, and tools that manage addresses and DNS together. But none of these is a complete solution on its own.

sections.title: Key Gaps in Automation
sections.content:
Despite existing tools, significant gaps remain. Many SLAAC and DHCPv6 interactions are ambiguous. When both are available in the same network, hosts behave unpredictably depending on OS implementation. The M and O flags in RA messages are advisory, not prescriptive, leading to different behavior on different systems.

DNS record updates do not automatically synchronize with host address changes. Secure Dynamic DNS (DDNS) can help, but requires key management and is usually performed by DHCP servers rather than hosts. For SLAAC hosts, triggering DNS updates is difficult.

Address-relevant configuration is scattered: firewalls have Access Control Lists, routers have policies, servers have hardcoded addresses, and monitoring systems store IP-to-device mappings. There is no centralized mechanism to update all of these simultaneously. Some devices support parameterized configuration (using variables), but most require manual updates to each place an address appears.
sections.plainLanguage: Computers don't always agree on how to get addresses from SLAAC and DHCP. DNS records don't automatically update when addresses change. And firewall rules, server settings, and monitoring logs all have addresses that need updating manually.

sections.title: Renumbering Event Management
sections.content:
Managing a renumbering event as a network-wide operation requires several functions currently missing. Hosts and servers need notification of upcoming renumbering so they can be ready. DNS caches need to be flushed when DNS records change; there should be a notification mechanism for this. Border routers need to know when renumbering happens in adjacent domains so they can update filters. Ingress filters at ISP interfaces need to know about new legitimate prefixes when a multihomed site renumbers.

Network Management Systems (NMS) that collect logs and monitor devices need to learn the mapping between old and new addresses for each host, so they don't treat the new address as a new device. DNS update synchronization is challenging because of Time To Live (TTL) latency: if DNS TTL is too long, the old address information persists longer than needed.

Currently, there is no standard mechanism for monitoring renumbering success. For stateless operations like SLAAC, it is difficult to determine whether all hosts have configured new addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: When renumbering happens, many systems need to be told about it: DNS servers, monitoring systems, firewalls, and others. Some of these notifications should happen before the change, some during, and some after. There is no standard way to coordinate all of this.

sections.title: Fundamental Limitations
sections.content:
Some gaps are architectural and difficult or impossible to solve. Transport-layer protocols (TCP, UDP) are rigidly bound to IP address pairs; changing addresses breaks existing connections. This is fundamental to how IP works and cannot easily be changed. Applications that cache addresses face similar issues: they must validate addresses when using them.

DNS has authority issues: if hosted servers have DNS records maintained by external parties, the hosting provider cannot unilaterally update those records during renumbering. This is an operational and policy issue without a technical solution.

IPv6 RA prefix lifetimes cannot be reduced below 2 hours when the current lifetime exceeds that, as a denial-of-service protection. This can slow down renumbering when the old prefix lifetime was set very long.

Multicast renumbering is complex. For unicast-prefix-based multicast addresses, the multicast address must change if the unicast prefix changes, requiring application reconfiguration. For Source-Specific Multicast, receivers must learn new source addresses, which is application-dependent.
sections.plainLanguage: Some problems are hard to fix because they are baked into how the Internet works. Network connections are tied to address pairs, so changing addresses breaks them. DNS authority is a business issue, not a technical one. And multicast is tricky because applications hardcode addresses.
